opening.headline: The discrepancy between slow answers to simple questions and shallow answers to difficult problems is explained by the difference between the inference model and model rating, and a selection criterion appropriate for the task is established.
body: We use the same AI tool, but simple tasks such as organizing today's meeting times require a long wait, and planning problems with many conditions are sometimes returned with a two-line shallow answer. This misalignment is usually caused by a mismatch between the task and the model.

In this class, before answering, we will first look at how the inference model and general model are different, and how the model classes divided into large, medium, and light achieve a balance between speed, cost, and quality. Next, you will select the appropriate grade for the three tasks with evidence and learn the standards for judging whether the evidence is appropriate.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the differences between inference models, general models, and large, medium, and light classes
You can distinguish between grades appropriate for task difficulty and delay time.
You can determine whether the basis for model selection is appropriate

screens.title: Slow answers to simple questions and shallow answers to difficult problems
screens.lead: We show the two situations divided into tabs. Select and read each tab, and see how the two situations connect in the last tab.

visual.alt: Two situation cards with simple questions and long wait times on the top and difficult questions and short answers on the bottom.
labels: Create a plan that takes into account schedule, budget, and manpower constraints

tabs.label: Situation 1
tabs.body: It's a simple question, but the answer came late. It was a request to summarize today's meeting time in one line, which I found in the email, but I had to wait for a while to get an answer. This can happen if the user expects a quick answer, but you are using a model that takes a long time to think.

tabs.label: Situation 2
tabs.body: It is a planning problem with many conditions intertwined, but it returns a shallow two-line answer. This is a problem that requires solving schedule, budget, and manpower constraints, but this is a case where the model provides general advice without examining it in depth. This can occur in models geared toward quick answers or in settings that involve little thought.

tabs.label: diagnosis
tabs.body:
Although the two situations seem opposite, the cause is the same. The difficulty of the task and the nature of the model do not match. Firstly, the model was too heavy for the task and secondly, the model was too light for the task.

There is only one question in this class. How do you choose the right model for the job?

screens.outro: First, let's think about what criteria you usually use to select a model.

screens.title: Think of fast models, smart models, and standards
screens.lead: Read the questions below and organize the answers in your head. There are no fields to enter or submit.

visual.alt: Illustration of a scale with speed and depth on both sides.
labels: What am I trying to do?

paragraphs: If there is a “fast model” and a “smart model,” by what criteria should one choose one? If you've ever chosen someone based on their name or reputation, think about the reason why.

Ask yourself the following three things to organize your thoughts. What I'm going to do today has to be done in how many seconds. How big is the cost of having to redo it if you make a mistake? How many times do you repeat the same thing a day?

There is no correct answer, and you will not receive an answer on this screen. Just compare how close your answers to the three questions above are to the criteria for selecting a model at the end of this lesson.

callout.label: Organizing the instructor's thoughts
callout.text: A fast model is not always better, nor is a smart model always better. The criteria are speed, cost, and the burden of being wrong. Weighing these three things to suit the task is model selection.

screens.outro: First, let's look at how the thinking and answering model differs from regular models.

screens.title: General and inferential models: Time to think
screens.lead: Press the switch to alternately compare the processing flow of the general model and the inference model.

visual.alt: Two flow charts: the general model goes directly from question to answer, and the inference model goes from question to thought to answer.
labels: Planning, exploring alternatives, checking intermediate results

states.label: regular model
states.body: When I am asked a question, I immediately start writing the answer. Because there are no additional thinking steps in between, responses are faster and less expensive. The simpler the question, the better this approach works. Conversely, problems that require multiple steps to be solved may result in shallow answers without intermediate checks because the answer must be given all at once. It's perfect for things like triaging simple inquiries that require fact-checking, polishing sentences, and short summaries.

states.label: inference model
states.body:
Before answering, an inference token is written internally. The OpenAI documentation explains that this process helps the model plan, explore alternatives, escape ambiguity, and solve more difficult multi-step problems. It is said to be particularly well-suited to complex problem solving, coding, scientific reasoning, and multi-step agent tasks.

The Claude article explains that during thinking, a model tries approaches, checks intermediate results, and discards paths that don't fit. This process requires additional resources. Tokens spent on Thoughts are charged as output tokens and also count toward your maximum output limit. Increasing inferences can improve accuracy for difficult problems, but it does not guarantee improvement and increases time and cost.

screens.outro: Inference models can also adjust the depth within a model. Let's take a look at those settings.

screens.title: Effort level to control depth
screens.lead: Move the slider to change your effort level. The explanation changes as to how speed and depth of response vary depending on the level.

stops.body: This is a setting that reduces thinking to a minimum. The fastest response and lowest cost. It is suitable for tasks that do not need to be examined in depth, such as simple classification, short extraction, and conversion to a fixed format. Using this level for difficult problems can result in shallow answers, as we saw earlier.

This setting is a compromise between speed and depth. It's a great starting point for most of your daily tasks. If the result is insufficient, raise it, and if it is sufficient, leave it as is or adjust it by lowering it. Rather than trying to find the right answer all at once, it is better to move step by step while looking at the results. This will both reduce unnecessary waiting time and costs.

Models think longer and more thoroughly. It is suitable for difficult tasks such as planning with many conditions or finding contradictions in long data. You'll have to deal with slower responses and increased costs due to thought tokens.

OpenAI provides reasoning effort levels from low to max, and Claude also sets an effort parameter that exchanges intelligence, latency, and cost within one model. Claude's model selection guide explains that adjusting effort before changing models is often a better tool. This means that you should first adjust the depth within the same model.

screens.outro: Now let's compare the models themselves in a table to see what grade they are divided into.

screens.title: Compare large, medium, and light grades in one table
screens.lead: The table below shows model overviews from the three companies side by side on the same basis. Read along the lines and compare the roles for each grade.

data.caption: Representative models and roles for each model grade of the three companies
rows: Gemini 4 Argon: Flagship inference model with integrated 1M context window
GPT-6 Astra: A representative model for complex reasoning and coding. $10 input, $50 output (per MTok)
Claude Fable 5.1: For demanding inference and long-term agent tasks. Speed is slow, input $10, output $50
Gemini 3.8 Flash: Flash family tailored for long-term software tasks and agents
GPT-6.1 Sol: Balancing intelligence and cost. Input $2, Output $10
Claude Sonnet 5.5: A combination of speed and intelligence. Speed is fast, input $2, output $10
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite: The fastest and most cost-effective high-volume processing
GPT-6 Luna: The most efficient model for intensive, high-volume tasks
Claude Haiku 5.5: For bulk tasks like sorting, extraction, and routing. The fastest speed, starting from $0.10
data.notes: What all three companies have in common is that larger models have higher prices and slower speeds. There's also the Opus 5.5 ($4 input, $20 output) on the Claude table, which falls between large and medium for long-duration agent coding and knowledge work. The context window is the total amount of tokens the model can see at one time. Pricing is based on 1 million tokens (MTok), and the lightweight tier of all three companies is designed to take on high-volume tasks at very low prices.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the standards in the table, let’s apply them to actual work.

screens.title: Commentary: Simple Classification and Contract Review
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the grades appropriate for the two tasks. Select the right arrow to advance one step at a time.

steps.title: Case 1: Inquiry mail classification
steps.body: Thousands of customer inquiry emails need to be divided into “Delivery,” “Refund,” and “Other.” There are three criteria for judgment. Is the output format simple with one label, is there a large number of cases, and does the response need to be fast? This case answers “yes” to all three questions.

steps.title: Case 1 Conclusion
steps.body: Since this is a simple, high-volume job, a lightweight grade is suitable. The Claude article also introduces Haiku as a model for high-volume tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing. If you use a deep-thinking model, the accuracy will remain the same, but time and cost will increase.

steps.title: Case 2: Contract Review
steps.body: You have to look for contradictions and exceptions between provisions in dozens of pages of contracts. The criteria for judgment are the same this time as well. You have to connect scattered clues in a long piece of material, missing a point is costly, and response time is relatively unimportant.

steps.title: Case 2 Conclusion
steps.body: A deep reasoning model or high level is correct. This is because the cost of error is high and it is a difficult task. In this case, rather than going with the most expensive model from the beginning, you can try increasing the effort first.

steps.title: Instructor's Evaluation Criteria
steps.body: What separates the two cases is not the name of the model, but three questions. How high are the accuracy requirements? How much delay is acceptable? How big is the cost of being wrong? Answering these three questions will naturally determine your grade.

screens.outro: The final example is a pyramid scheme, in which we will also determine whether the basis for selection is appropriate.

screens.title: Commentary: Developing a multi-step plan and assessing the basis for selection
screens.lead: When you select each item, the instructor's commentary unfolds. Think about it for yourself and then click to compare.

items.prompt: Case 3. Which model is appropriate for a new product launch plan that must address schedule, budget, and manpower constraints?
items.answer: A model that thinks deeply is appropriate. Since the constraints affect each other, it is easy to get confused if you give the answer all at once. Inference models are advantageous for these multi-step problems because they can attempt approaches, check intermediate results, and discard blocked paths.

items.prompt: Is the rationale “I will use the most expensive model because it is the best” appropriate?
items.answer: It's not appropriate. This is because the reason has nothing to do with the work. Expensive models come at the cost of being slower and more expensive, which can be detrimental to simple tasks.

items.prompt: Is the rationale “This task has high error costs and requires linking long data, so I will use a high grade” appropriate?
items.answer: Appropriate. This is because it touches on the selection criteria of task difficulty, delay tolerance, and error cost. The reason is given above in the balance of speed, cost and quality.

items.prompt: What if I'm not sure which model to start with?
items.answer: The Claude article suggests two ways to get started: Efficiency priority is to start with a lightweight model and raise it only when there are deficiencies, while ability priority is to start with the strongest model and later lower the effort or lower the model. The former is appropriate for large quantities and simple tasks, and the latter is appropriate for difficult tasks where accuracy is more important than cost.

An appropriate basis for selection should strike a balance between speed, cost and quality. You should be able to speak not by name or recognition, but by the difficulty of the task and the burden of being wrong.

screens.outro: I will organize the contents so far into key criteria.

screens.title: Criteria for choosing the right model for the job
screens.lead: We summarize what we have seen so far into one selection criterion.

paragraphs: The model lies between being expensive and slow instead of thinking deeply, and being cheap and fast instead of thinking shallowly. The inference model spends time thinking before answering, and the tokens it spends on thinking are also included in the cost as output tokens. Depth doesn't come for free.

So the choice starts from the task and not from the model's recognition. We ask in that order how difficult the task is, how fast the response should be, and how much it costs to try again if we make a mistake. We then change the model after first adjusting the depth using effort within the same model.

The two situations we saw at the beginning can also be reread on this basis. If you were slow on simple questions, it was because the model was too heavy, and if you were slow on difficult questions, it was because the model or settings were too light.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Choose a level based on the difficulty of the task, tolerance for delay, and cost of error. The most expensive model isn't always the answer.

glossary.def: This is a model that uses inference tokens internally to plan and look at alternatives before answering.
This is the inference step the model uses before coming up with a final answer. This takes time and costs output tokens.
It is a classification of models with different capabilities, speeds, and costs, such as large, medium, and light.
This is a setting that adjusts the balance of depth, delay, and cost within a model.

misconceptions.fact: For simple, high-volume tasks, larger models can be slow and expensive. A grade that matches the difficulty of the task and tolerance for delay is the best choice.

misconceptions.myth: Inference models are smarter without cost.
misconceptions.fact: Tokens spent on Thoughts are charged as output tokens and also count toward your maximum output limit. This adds time and money at the expense of gaining depth.

misconceptions.myth: Choosing a model is a matter of memorizing the name.
misconceptions.fact: Model names change frequently, but the standards are the same. If you choose based on task difficulty, latency, cost, and error cost, you can make a decision even if the name is different.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Instead of thinking deeply, models are divided into expensive and slow, and cheap and fast.
Inference models use thought tokens, which increases time and cost.
You can adjust the depth with effort even within the same model, and it's worth trying first before changing models.
Choose a level based on task difficulty, tolerance for delay, and cost of error.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What grade do I need for the most difficult tasks in my job? Explain why in terms of difficulty, delay, and cost of error.

checks.q: Which of the following is an appropriate explanation for 'tokens used while thinking' in the reasoning model?
options: Charged as an output token and included in the maximum output limit
There is no cost as it is not visible on the screen.
It is calculated only from input tokens and has nothing to do with output limits.
The more you think, the less time and money you save.
checks.explain: The inference model internally writes an inference token before answering, and this token is billed as an output token and also counts towards the maximum output limit. Instead of gaining depth, time and cost increase.

wrong.1: Even if it is not visible, it is included in the cost.
wrong.3: The more you think, the more time and money you spend.
